params: Earth peeks over the Moon’s horizon
earthrise.history: On 24 December 1968, on Apollo 8’s fourth orbit, Bill Anders saw Earth rise over the Moon and grabbed a colour film camera. His photo, Earthrise, became one of the most famous pictures ever taken.

eagle.history: On 20 July 1969 Neil Armstrong took manual control to fly past a boulder field. Eagle touched down with only about 25 seconds of fuel left before the abort limit.

home13.history: After an oxygen tank exploded in April 1970, the crew used the lunar module’s engine to swing around the Moon and come home. Small burns kept them inside the narrow entry window, and they splashed down safely on 17 April.

slingshot.history: Voyager 2 swung past Jupiter on 9 July 1979. Jupiter’s gravity bent its path and added speed, sending it on to Saturn in 1981 and later to Uranus and Neptune.

stars: Near and far points within 2,000 km
rohini.history: On 18 July 1980 India’s SLV-3 rocket put the 35 kg Rohini satellite into orbit from Sriharikota. The project director was Dr A.P.J. Abdul Kalam.

cassini.history: On 1 July 2004 Cassini flew through a gap in Saturn’s rings and fired its main engine for 96 minutes. It became the first spacecraft to orbit Saturn.

mip.history: On 14 November 2008 the Moon Impact Probe left Chandrayaan-1 and fell for about 25 minutes, hitting near Shackleton crater. Its instruments sniffed the thin gas around the Moon on the way down.

window.history: Mangalyaan launched on 5 November 2013. PSLV could not send it straight to Mars, so it raised its orbit six times and left Earth on 1 December, right inside the window.

escape.history: On 1 December 2013 Mangalyaan fired its engine for about 22 minutes near perigee and left Earth on its way to Mars.

marscapture.history: On 24 September 2014 Mangalyaan braked for about 23 minutes behind Mars. India became the first country to reach Mars orbit on its first attempt.

pluto.history: New Horizons flew past Pluto on 14 July 2015. The flyby was programmed in advance, and the photos took months to send home across 5 billion km.

juno.history: On 4 July 2016 Juno fired its main engine for 35 minutes and became the second spacecraft ever to orbit Jupiter.

sats104.history: On 15 February 2017 PSLV-C37 released 104 satellites in about 11 minutes, each in a planned direction so none would ever collide. It was a world record at the time.

terror.history: On 18 February 2021 Perseverance entered Mars’s air at about 19,500 km/h. A supersonic parachute opened, the heat shield dropped away, and a rocket-powered sky crane lowered the rover into Jezero crater on cables.

raise.history: After launch on 14 July 2023, Chandrayaan-3 raised its orbit five times, always burning near perigee where each push counts most.

moonshot.history: On 1 August 2023 Chandrayaan-3 made its trans-lunar injection burn at perigee and left Earth orbit for the Moon.

catchmoon.history: On 5 August 2023 Chandrayaan-3 braked for about 30 minutes and was captured into a lunar orbit, then lowered it step by step to about 100 km.

vikram.history: On 23 August 2023 Vikram landed near the Moon’s south pole. India became the first country to land there and the fourth to soft-land on the Moon.

hop.history: On 3 September 2023 Vikram fired its engines, rose about 40 cm and landed 30–40 cm away: a test for future missions that must lift off from the Moon.

spadex.history: On 16 January 2025 ISRO’s two SpaDeX satellites docked in orbit. India became the fourth country to dock spacecraft in space.

sre1.history: SRE-1 launched on 10 January 2007 and spent 12 days in orbit. On 22 January it fired its de-boost motor, hit the air at about 8 km/s and came down on parachutes in the Bay of Bengal, where it was recovered: India’s first spacecraft to return from orbit.
sre1.note: The target is drawn where it will be when you arrive (Earth turns a little during the fall).

astrosat.history: AstroSat launched on 28 September 2015 on PSLV-C30. It is India’s first multi-wavelength space observatory, studying stars, galaxies and black holes in ultraviolet, visible and X-ray light at the same time.

dodge.history: ISRO predicted that Chandrayaan-2’s orbiter and NASA’s LRO would pass within about 3 km of each other over the Moon’s north pole on 20 October 2021, with less than 100 m between their orbits. A small burn on 18 October moved the orbiter safely out of the way.

navic.history: NavIC is India’s own satellite navigation system, like GPS. NVS-01, launched on 29 May 2023 on GSLV-F12, was the first of its second generation and carries an Indian-made atomic clock.

stars: With 2.5 t of cryogenic fuel left
lvm3.history: On 14 July 2023 LVM3-M4 lifted off from Sriharikota. Its two S200 boosters, the L110 core and the C25 cryogenic stage placed Chandrayaan-3 into a 170 × 36,500 km orbit about 16 minutes later.
lvm3.note: Air drag is left out to keep the level short.

hazard.history: On 23 August 2023, at about 150 m above the Moon, Vikram paused to scan the ground with its hazard-detection cameras. The spot below was not safe, so it moved sideways to a safer place before touching down.

pragyan.history: On 27 August 2023 Pragyan’s cameras spotted a 4 m wide crater 3 m ahead. ISRO commanded it to back up and take a new path. Pragyan drove about 100 m on the Moon before the lunar night.

stars: Stay in the zone for one loop
aditya.history: Aditya-L1 launched on 2 September 2023 and entered its halo orbit around L1 on 6 January 2024. From there it watches the Sun without ever being blocked by Earth or the Moon.
aditya.note: Shown flat (in 2D); the real halo orbit also loops above and below.

insat.history: INSAT-3DS launched on 17 February 2024 on GSLV-F14. From its slot at 82°E it watches India’s weather, cyclones and clouds day and night.

pushpak.vehicle: Pushpak RLV-LEX-03 (dropped by a Chinook helicopter)
pushpak.history: On 23 June 2024 a Chinook helicopter released Pushpak 4.5 km up. It glided down on its own, landed at about 320 km/h on the runway at Chitradurga and stopped with a brake parachute and wheel brakes.
